keyword: react vs wordpress for business website
title: React vs WordPress for Business Websites: What You're Actually Choosing
excerpt: Most people compare React and WordPress like they're alternatives. They're not. Understanding what you're really choosing will save you from an expensive mistake.

blocks.text: You've probably seen the debate online: React vs WordPress. Maybe a developer told you to use React. Maybe you've heard WordPress is outdated. Maybe you've heard the opposite.

Here's the problem with that debate: it's comparing the wrong things. React and WordPress don't solve the same problem. Comparing them directly is like comparing a kitchen knife to a restaurant — one is a tool, the other is a system built around many tools.
Once you understand what each actually is, the real decision becomes clear — and you'll be able to make it without needing a developer to interpret it for you.
What WordPress Actually Is

WordPress is a Content Management System (CMS) — software that lets you build and manage a website through a browser-based dashboard, without writing code. It was launched in 2003 and today powers roughly 43% of all websites on the internet.

Under the hood, it runs PHP (a programming language) on a server and queries a database every time someone loads a page. You install plugins to add features — contact forms, SEO tools, e-commerce, analytics. You install themes to control the design.
WordPress is good for:

items: Content-heavy sites where a non-technical team needs to publish regularly
Blogs, news sites, or magazines with frequent updates
Quick setups where time-to-launch is the priority
E-commerce via WooCommerce if your catalogue isn't too complex
Situations where your team already knows WordPress

blocks.text: The promise of WordPress is autonomy: once set up, you can run your own website without a developer. That promise is real — with an important asterisk we'll get to.
What React Actually Is

React is a JavaScript library created by Meta (Facebook) in 2013. It's used to build the interactive parts of a web page — buttons, menus, forms, dynamic content. By itself, React is not a website. It has no server, no routing, no content management, and no way to deploy itself.

This is the source of most confusion. When people say "React website", they almost always mean a site built with **Next.js** — a framework built on top of React that adds everything React is missing: server-side rendering, page routing, image optimisation, deployment infrastructure, and more.
Think of it this way: React is an engine. Next.js is the car. You can't drive an engine, but you can drive the car.

A Next.js site is written in code by a developer. Pages are built at deployment time (not on every page load), served as ultra-fast static files from a global content delivery network, and deployed automatically whenever code changes. There's no dashboard for editing content — unless one is added separately.
The Real Question: CMS vs Custom Development
Once you understand what both tools actually are, the comparison reframes itself. The real choice isn't React vs WordPress. It's this:
**Do you want a managed CMS (WordPress, Webflow, Squarespace) — or a custom-built site on a modern framework (Next.js)?**

A CMS gives you a dashboard, ready-made templates, and the ability to edit your own content without a developer. The trade-off is that you're working within a system someone else designed, with limits on performance, customisation, and security.

A custom-built site gives you complete control over performance, design, and functionality. The trade-off is higher upfront development cost and, without a connected content editor, you'll need a developer for content changes.
Neither is wrong. The right answer depends on your priorities.
Honest Comparison
Let's put both options side by side on the things that actually matter for a business website:

rows: Minimal — no database, no PHP, no admin panel
Low for content, high for custom features
Unlimited — any feature is possible in code
Near zero — no plugins or PHP to maintain

blocks.text: Who Should Use WordPress
WordPress is still the right choice in some specific situations. Consider it if:

items: Your team needs to publish content daily or several times a week, and doing that through a developer is not viable
You run a content-heavy site — a news outlet, a magazine, a blog with dozens of authors
Your budget is tight and you already have WordPress expertise in-house
You're running a WooCommerce store and your e-commerce needs fit what WooCommerce offers out of the box
Your site's primary purpose is content, not conversion or performance

blocks.text: If your situation is primarily about managing a lot of content with a small team and limited budget, WordPress can work well. The problems tend to emerge once performance, security, or growth become priorities.
Who Should Use React / Next.js
A Next.js site is the better investment if any of the following are true:

items: Performance matters to your business — you're investing in SEO or paid traffic where load speed directly affects rankings and conversion rates
Security is non-negotiable — you work in professional services, finance, healthcare, or any field where a compromised website is more than just an inconvenience
You need custom integrations — CRM connections, booking systems, industry-specific APIs that no plugin covers
You're growing beyond what plugins can handle — your WordPress site has become a stack of workarounds
You're thinking long-term — the total cost of ownership over 3 years often favours Next.js once you account for plugin licences, developer call-out costs, and maintenance

blocks.text: The Hidden Costs of WordPress
WordPress is marketed as free. The software itself is. But the real cost of running a business WordPress site is rarely as low as the initial quote suggests.
Here's what a typical business WordPress site actually costs per year:

rows: SEO plugin (Yoast Premium, Rank Math Pro)
Form builder, backup plugin, other essentials
Developer time for updates, breaks, custom fixes

blocks.text: That doesn't include the time your team spends on updates, the cost of a security incident if one occurs, or the revenue lost from slow page speeds during the months before you notice a problem.
The 'free' CMS has a real total cost. It's just distributed across many line items, which makes it easy to miss.
The Hidden Costs of React / Next.js
A Next.js site isn't without its own trade-offs. Be honest about these before you decide:

items: **Higher upfront development cost.** A custom-built Next.js site costs more than a WordPress site to build from scratch. You're paying for code quality, not a template.

**No off-the-shelf plugins.** Every feature — contact form, booking system, newsletter — is either built, integrated via API, or sourced from a third-party service. There's no plugin marketplace to browse.

**Developer needed for content changes** (unless you connect a headless CMS like Sanity, Contentful, or similar). If your developer is unavailable, you can't update a phone number without their help — unless this is planned for upfront.

blocks.text: The last point is solvable. A headless CMS can be connected to a Next.js site to give you an editing dashboard for content while keeping all the performance and security advantages. It adds cost and complexity to the build, but eliminates the dependency on a developer for day-to-day content.
The Bottom Line
Here's a simple framework for deciding:

items: **You need to edit content yourself every day, and you can't wait for a developer** → Consider WordPress, or build a Next.js site with a headless CMS connected from day one.
**Performance, security, and long-term cost efficiency matter** → Next.js is the better investment. The upfront cost is higher; the ongoing cost and risk are lower.

**You're not sure** → Run your current site through a performance check first. If your PageSpeed score is below 60 on mobile, your WordPress installation is already costing you in SEO rankings and lost conversions.

blocks.text: The decision isn't really about React vs WordPress. It's about what your website is for, who needs to manage it, and what you're willing to invest now versus later.

A website that looks cheap to build but costs you in slow traffic, missed leads, and monthly plugin subscriptions isn't actually cheap. And a custom-built site that performs at 95+ on mobile and never needs a security patch might be the better business decision — even if the invoice is higher.
